newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Focus-S&P "raised outlook" rewards Swedish budget.
newsitem.headline: Focus-S&P "raised outlook" rewards Swedish budget.

text.p: U.S. credit rating agency Standard & Poor's (S&P) honoured Swedish budget austerity on Friday by raising its outlook for the country to stable from negative.

S&P, which affirmed the country's longterm credit rating at AA+, said an upgrade or even a positive outlook for the Kingdom of Sweden ratings was contingent upon substantial progress in lowering the fiscal debt programme.

"The change in the foreign currency rating outlook reflects the improvement in the government's fiscal and balance of payments flexibility as the general government deficit continues to narrow and the high governmental debt burden edges down," S&P said in a statement.
The agency said it was affirming its outlook for the longterm local currency rating at stable. It affirmed the longterm local currency credit rating at AAA and shortterm debt ratings at A-1+.
Interest rates eased immediately and the crown moved to 4.46 against the mark versus 4.48 immediately before the announcement.
"It's obvious this is positive. Now expectations of a rating upgrade are rising," one Stockholm crown trader said.

Sweden earlier this week announced an expansive budget for the next four years which involves spending more than 60 billion crowns on restoring some welfare services after two and a half years of tough cutbacks.

"The higher local currency rating reflects the government's success in fiscal consolidation, its flexibility in taxing and influence over monetary matters and its commitment to and success in achieving low inflation," S&P said.
S&P said success in pursuing the twin goals of fiscal consolidation and creating employment depended on modest wage settlements and improved labour market flexibility.
Pension reform would also be important in keeping fiscal balances in check over the longer term.

Continued high unemployment, running at 8.4 percent in March, has eroded the minority Social Democratic government's popularity and elections in September 1998 could bring a more broadly based coalition government for which fiscal restraint could be more difficult, the rating agency said.

"However the importance of fiscal restraint in improving competitiveness and remaining in line with European Monetary Union objectives suggests that any new government will avoid reverting to high fiscal imbalances," S&P said.
